articles.title: What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?
articles.summary: It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved
articles.content:
It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

Bernhard Riemann set out a problem mathematicians have been trying solve for more than a century The Granger Collection/Alamy

The cadence of prime numbers has a pattern; it isn’t simply chaos. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven, and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions.

In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago.

“This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. The proof of the Reimann hypothesis is also one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million prize for a solution.

Advertisement

The Riemann hypothesis has loomed so large over mathematicians for decades because it concerns mathematics’ most simple yet hard-to-understand objects: prime numbers. These are numbers that aren’t divisible by any number other than 1 and themselves, and any number can be built by multiplying primes. In this way, primes are the bones of all systems of numbers; everything is built on top of them. But how primes are distributed among all numbers is, on the face of it, unpredictable. This is where Riemann made an intervention.

He hypothesised that the way primes are spaced throughout the number line can be inferred from another set of numbers, now tied to a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. These numbers are complex – so each is actually a pair of numbers, one called real and one called imaginary – and when they are plugged into the Riemann zeta function, the function spits out zero. Confusingly, these numbers that result in a zero from the function are called “non-trivial zeros”. Riemann discovered that summing over a sequence of these complex numbers allowed him to predict the distribution of primes up to a certain high number. Effectively, he came upon a formula that could make sense of primes’ seemingly random appearances among numbers.

But the formula only works if all the zeros always sit on the same vertical line when plotted in a coordinate system where the horizontal axis tracks their real number constituents and the vertical axis their imaginary ones. Riemann calculated some of these zeros, which confirmed his idea, but could not prove the hypothesis more generally. It became the biggest unsolved problem in all of mathematics. “It is a legendary problem, the queen of all the Millennium Problems,” says Scott Armstrong at Sorbonne University in Paris. “For the whole field of mathematics, there could not be a bigger theorem.”

In the intervening years, mathematicians used computers to verify that the first 12 trillion nontrivial zeros line up on Riemann’s vertical line and much work has gone into proving that the zeros at least must lie in a strip of the coordinate systems around this line. In fact, a previous release of AI proofs by OpenAI on 6 October contained the proof of a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, placing the non-trivial zeros in the neighbourhood but not exactly on the line Riemann predicted.

In a statement released to the public, Alpöge wrote that his proof, developed with Anthropic’s Claude AI, is over 250,000 pages long, and it has not yet been fully read, digested or understood by the mathematics community. Even its translation into the language of the proof-checking software Lean is 17,000,000 lines long. That means it will take time to carefully adjudicate. “I have not had a chance to read the 17 million lines of Lean, so cannot speak to their truth,” says Alex Walker at University College London. And the announcement didn’t illuminate the details of the method, he adds.

Consequently, it is currently unclear exactly what mathematical tricks the AI leveraged, though early commentators suggest that it drew on a vast swathe of mathematics spanning several fields including number theory and arithmetic geometry. Some have suggested the AI made connections across these fields that don’t already clearly exist in the literature.

The Lean code is in the process of being adapted to efficiently run on a computer that can review it, which will provide a crucial check on the new proof. “While Lean itself has some issues, so far none of the AI results with Lean certificates have had to be retracted,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin. Still, it may take years to unravel all the details of the new proof and reap any of its mathematical insights, he says. But the ramifications will certainly be enormous and extensive.

Notably, it resolves the biggest open question of number theory by finally making primes make sense. Numerous results also build on the assumption that Riemann was right and will now stand on firmer ground. And then there are implications for functions similar to the Riemann zeta function, known as the generalised Riemann hypothesis. “An extremely large number of results have previously been proven subject to the generalised Riemann hypothesis,” says John Nicholson at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Germany. He says there are also a number of fast algorithms for computing quantities in algebraic number theory whose correctness depends on the generalised Riemann hypothesis. The Riemann hypothesis even has ties to theories of chaos in quantum systems in physics.

“The failure of the Riemann hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers,” wrote Enrico Bombieri at Princeton University when outlining the Millenium Problem more than a quarter of a century ago. Now, thanks to a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, that distribution may have been shown to be not that dangerous after all.

This achievement has broad significance for mathematics and related fields, offering deep insights into number theory and potentially impacting physics and computing. The story focuses on this single, substantial scientific advancement with detailed context, fulfilling the criteria for inspiring good news.

articles.title: A decades-old mystery about light could hold the key to faster internet
articles.summary: A promising material for ultra-fast optical communications has held a secret for decades, but scientists may have finally cracked it. Researchers at KAIST and Caltech have precisely measured how barium titanate controls and absorbs light, resolving longstanding uncertainties that have slowed its development. Their findings could make it easier to build optical devices that transmit information faster while wasting less light.
articles.content:
Light can carry vast amounts of information, but developing faster and more efficient optical communication systems requires precise control over how it travels. Scientists have now made an important advance in understanding barium titanate (BTO), a promising material that could help improve the performance of future devices that transmit information using light.

A research team led by KAIST has uncovered detailed information about how light moves through BTO and how much of it the material absorbs. These properties have been difficult to measure accurately for decades because of the crystal's complicated internal structure. The new findings provide engineers with a more reliable foundation for designing optical devices that minimize signal loss and support faster data transmission.

KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced the results on November 8. The research was led by Professor Min Seok Jang of KAIST's School of Electrical Engineering, working with Professor Harry A. Atwater's group at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), and U.S.-based J.A. Woollam Co. Together, the researchers examined how BTO interacts with light across wavelengths extending from the ultraviolet to the far-infrared.

Why Barium Titanate Could Transform Optical Communications

One of BTO's most valuable characteristics is its ability to change how it affects light when electricity is applied. This behavior, called the Pockels effect, gives the material a strong electro-optic response and makes it especially attractive for optical modulators. These components convert electrical information into signals carried by light, making them important building blocks for advanced communication systems.

However, producing reliable devices requires a detailed understanding of two fundamental optical properties. The refractive index describes how light travels through a material, while the extinction coefficient indicates how strongly the material absorbs it. Engineers need both measurements to predict how light will behave inside a waveguide, a structure designed to direct light along a specific path, and how much of the optical signal may be lost.

Getting consistent measurements from BTO has been surprisingly challenging. The material can contain multiple microscopic regions, called domains, in which the crystal structure points in different directions. Because these regions interact with light differently, measurements of an entire sample can combine several distinct responses. This has contributed to widely conflicting reports of BTO's optical properties over many decades.

Solving a Decades-Old Mystery About Light

To overcome this problem, the researchers used a sophisticated measurement method known as Mueller matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry. The technique examines how the polarization of light changes when light reflects from or passes through a material, allowing scientists to investigate its optical behavior in detail.

Rather than relying on crystals containing a complicated mixture of differently oriented regions, the team studied two types of single-crystal samples with relatively consistent domain orientations. This approach helped minimize overlapping optical responses and allowed the researchers to identify the material's underlying properties more accurately.

Their measurements spanned wavelengths from 190 nanometers (nm) to 40 micrometers (μm), covering an exceptionally broad range of light from ultraviolet to far-infrared. Since a material's optical behavior changes with wavelength, the scientists divided the spectrum into three regions and applied a different analytical approach to each. This revealed how BTO's refractive index and light absorption depend on both wavelength and crystal orientation.

The researchers also investigated a particularly important range in which BTO allows nearly all incoming light to pass through. By combining ellipsometry with separate measurements of light transmission, they detected extremely low absorption, determining extinction coefficients of approximately 10-5 in the 2-10 μm wavelength range. These precise values will help engineers estimate how much light is lost as it travels through or remains confined within optical components.

In another advance, the team developed a way to predict the combined optical behavior of crystals containing multiple domains. Their method uses the orientations of those domains and the proportion of the crystal occupied by each to calculate the material's overall response to light.

Opening the Door to Faster Data Transmission and Quantum Technology

The results could make the development of future optical devices more predictable and efficient. With accurate information about BTO's behavior, engineers can model how light will travel through components of different shapes and dimensions before manufacturing them. They can also better estimate absorption losses, potentially reducing the need for repeated prototypes, costly redesigns, and extensive testing.

The potential benefits extend beyond conventional optical communications. BTO could also play an important role in devices that produce light at different wavelengths, as well as photonic circuits that use light to process quantum information. Such technologies depend on controlling light with exceptional precision.

"This study reveals the optical response of barium titanate, which had long remained unclear, and provides a reliable reference for how the material interacts with light," said Professor Min Seok Jang.

Jang also emphasized that the findings could contribute to optical communication devices capable of transmitting data faster while reducing light loss. The improved understanding of BTO may also support the development of quantum photonic technologies, where precise manipulation of light is essential.

The study was published online on October 20, 2026, in ACS Photonics. Jiwon Kang, a Ph.D. candidate in KAIST's School of Electrical Engineering, and Dr. Nina Hong of J.A. Woollam Co. served as co-first authors. Professors Min Seok Jang of KAIST and Harry A. Atwater of Caltech were the corresponding authors.

Funding was provided through the Culture, Sports and Tourism R&D Program administered by the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), with support from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism; the Basic Science Research Program administered by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), with support from the Ministry of Education; the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR).

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de KAIST, Caltech et d’autres instituts ont utilisé une méthode spéciale appelée ellipsométrie spectroscopique à matrice de Mueller pour étudier des cristaux de BTO avec des structures plus uniformes. articles.personality_title_es: Científicos resuelven misterio de la luz en titanio de bario para acelerar Internet
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La luz transmite información en la comunicación óptica, pero mejorar la velocidad y eficiencia depende de controlar cómo viaja la luz a través de los materiales. El titanio de bario (BTO) es un material prometedor, pero sus propiedades ópticas han sido difíciles de medir con precisión durante décadas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de KAIST, Caltech y otros institutos usaron un método especial llamado elipsometría espectroscópica con matriz de Mueller para estudiar cristales de BTO con estructuras más uniformes. Midieron cómo BTO cambia y absorbe la luz en un amplio rango de longitudes de onda, desde ultravioleta hasta infrarrojo lejano. Esto les permitió determinar con precisión dos propiedades clave: cómo la luz se dobla en BTO (índice de refracción) y cuánto la absorbe (coeficiente de extinción).

**Impacto** – Estas mediciones precisas solucionan un problema antiguo causado por la estructura compleja del BTO, que hacía que los datos anteriores fueran poco confiables. Ahora los ingenieros pueden diseñar mejor dispositivos ópticos, como moduladores, que convierten señales eléctricas en señales de luz con menos pérdida. Esto podría llevar a conexiones de internet más rápidas y mejores dispositivos que usan luz para comunicación o computación cuántica.

**Próximo paso** – Con este nuevo conocimiento, los ingenieros podrán crear componentes ópticos más eficientes y reducir costosos ensayos y errores en la producción. Los hallazgos también abren la puerta a mejores circuitos fotónicos para tecnologías cuánticas, donde controlar la luz con mucha precisión es fundamental.

**Resumen en una frase** – Al descubrir cómo el titanio de bario controla la luz, los científicos han allanado el camino para una comunicación óptica más rápida y tecnologías avanzadas basadas en la luz.

articles.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
articles.summary: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.
articles.content:
After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played important roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

The elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

It also creates new opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics

The LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

When particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of new forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

According to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale."

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth."

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

"We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons."

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

This name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from currently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

For now, the new measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

"There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.

"The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data."

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

Researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to important advances in understanding nature.

"This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success."

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful new way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

articles.title: Quantum effect could reverse gravity and violate Einstein’s theory of relativity
articles.summary: Two mathematical investigations devised a way to possibly make gravity produce repulsion between objects, breaking away from a long-standing understanding of this force
articles.content:
Two mathematical investigations devised a way to possibly make gravity produce repulsion between objects, breaking away from a long-standing understanding of this force

It might be possible to turn gravity into a force of repulsion, not attraction DOK/Alamy

Flying in the face of Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity, quantum physics could turn the famous force repulsive instead of attractive – and we could soon test the idea in the lab.

A hallmark of gravity as we know it is that it pulls objects with mass together: gravity explains why the moon orbits Earth, and why an apple falls to the ground after detaching from the tree. While this is well established, there is still no agreement on how gravity works at scales dominated by quantum effects, and what quantum properties it may have.

Now, two research teams have independently found that quantum effects can make gravity act repulsively, pushing objects apart instead of pulling them together.

Advertisement

“Gravity is always attractive – this has been the cornerstone of gravity from Newton to Einstein,” says Pablo Saldanha at the Federal University of Minas Gerais in Brazil, who worked on one of the studies with Vlatko Vedral and Chiara Marletto, both at the University of Oxford. “Anti-gravity or repulsion: no one has seen that before,” says Sougato Bose at University College London, who co-authored the other study with Lev Vaidman at Tel Aviv University in Israel.

A key concept for both studies was that of a quantum superposition state. Consider a car driving down a city street. When it arrives at an intersection where one road forks into two, it can take either the left or the right branch. But a quantum car would have another option: to enter a superposition of taking the left road and also the right one, assuming a state where it is impossible to tell where the car is exactly without disturbing it.

Another quantum object, called a “probe”, moving along a path parallel to both the left and right road branches, would be gravitationally attracted to the car. In both new studies, the researchers mathematically modelled an analogous setup and used equations to show that this gravitational interaction would make the car and the probe inextricably connected through the link of quantum entanglement.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Lost in Space-Time Sign up to newsletter

The two teams mathematically examined a scenario equivalent to the two roads – left and right – merging some time after they had split apart. At this point, a measurement taken by the probe can reveal how each of the paths shaped the superposed car’s quantum state.

Quantum mechanics is probabilistic. This means that if this experiment is repeated many times, the final state of the car won’t always be the same, but will follow some distribution of states instead, reflecting its capacity to follow a combination of the left and right branches. The researchers in both experiments found that if all but some specific states were then discarded after the measurement – a technique called post-selection, partly pioneered by Vaidman – then the probe should theoretically experience gravitational repulsion and be pushed away from the car in the experiment. “That repulsion, that going away [from the superposed object], is created at the time of the measurement,” says Bose.

Even Einstein’s theory of general relativity, which has for over a century proven to be an incredibly accurate description of gravity, doesn’t predict this kind of gravitational repulsion. “There is a measurement that will somehow conditionally give you repulsive gravitational force,” says Vedral. Confirmation that such a repulsive force occurs would demonstrate the quantum nature of gravity.

Because this measurement effect is inherently quantum, just like the possibility of a superposition state is, the scenario the two teams explored doesn’t have any non-quantum analogues. But it could still be tested in experiments.

Objects that can stay in a superposition state for the duration of an experiment would have to be very small, says Bose, and yet also still massive enough for gravity to make a difference to their behaviour. Bacterium-sized objects should do the trick. He and Vaidman calculated that the probe object at this scale would experience acceleration roughly smaller than a quadrillionth of gravitational acceleration on Earth. Vedral says that he and his colleagues are already working with experimentalists who specialise in unusually large quantum objects.

Tomasz Paterek at the University of Gdańsk in Poland says that the new idea is “brilliant”. Past studies explored making the force between electrons attractive, even though it is usually repulsive, through post-selection. But this is the first time that the same process has been shown to potentially reverse gravity’s character too, he says. In Paterek’s view, lab experiments that use gravity to quantum entangle objects could be achievable in the near future – but he cautions they will be really difficult to perform.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in understanding gravity through quantum physics, proposing that gravity could be repulsive under certain quantum conditions. This challenges long-standing theories and opens the door for experimental verification, representing a major advancement in fundamental physics with broad implications for science and technology.
articles.personality_title: Scientists find quantum way to make gravity push instead of pull
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Gravity is known as a force that pulls objects together, like the Earth pulling the moon or an apple falling from a tree. This idea comes from famous scientists like Newton and Einstein. But scientists have not fully understood how gravity works when very tiny things, like particles, are involved.

**What happened** – Two research teams from Brazil, the UK, and Israel used math to show that under special quantum conditions, gravity might push objects apart instead of pulling them together. They imagined a situation where a tiny object takes two paths at once, a strange idea from quantum physics called superposition. Another object nearby would feel gravity differently because of this. Their calculations showed that if they carefully pick certain outcomes in the experiment, gravity could become repulsive.

**Impact** – This idea challenges the long-held belief that gravity only attracts. It also suggests that gravity has quantum properties, which scientists have been trying to prove for a long time. If tested and confirmed in the lab, this could change how we understand the universe and lead to new technologies based on quantum gravity.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to test this idea with very small objects, about the size of bacteria, that can stay in superposition long enough for gravity to act. These experiments are very hard but possible with current technology. Scientists are already working with experts who study big quantum objects to try and observe this repulsive gravity.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New mathematical research shows that quantum physics might let gravity push objects apart, offering a way to test the quantum nature of gravity in future experiments.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques découvrent comment la gravité pourrait repousser au lieu d’attirer grâce à la physique quantique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La gravité est connue comme une force qui attire les objets, comme la Terre qui attire la Lune ou une pomme qui tombe d’un arbre. Cette idée vient de scientifiques célèbres comme Newton et Einstein. Mais on ne comprend pas encore bien comment la gravité fonctionne avec les objets très petits, comme les particules.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Deux équipes de recherche du Brésil, du Royaume-Uni et d’Israël ont utilisé des mathématiques pour montrer que, dans certaines conditions quantiques, la gravité pourrait repousser les objets au lieu de les attirer. Ils ont imaginé une situation où un objet minuscule prend deux chemins en même temps, une idée étrange de la physique quantique appelée superposition. Un autre objet proche ressentirait la gravité différemment à cause de cela. Leurs calculs montrent que si on choisit certains résultats dans l’expérience, la gravité pourrait devenir répulsive.

**Impact** – Cette idée remet en cause la croyance que la gravité attire toujours. Elle suggère aussi que la gravité a des propriétés quantiques, ce que les scientifiques cherchent à prouver depuis longtemps. Si on le confirme en laboratoire, cela pourrait changer notre compréhension de l’univers et ouvrir la voie à de nouvelles technologies basées sur la gravité quantique.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent tester cette idée avec des objets très petits, de la taille d’une bactérie, qui peuvent rester en superposition assez longtemps pour que la gravité agisse. Ces expériences sont difficiles mais possibles avec la technologie actuelle. Des scientifiques travaillent déjà avec des experts des grands objets quantiques pour essayer d’observer cette gravité répulsive.

**Une phrase pour résumer** – De nouvelles recherches mathématiques montrent que la physique quantique pourrait permettre à la gravité de repousser les objets, ouvrant une voie pour tester la nature quantique de la gravité dans de futures expériences.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren cómo la gravedad podría empujar en lugar de atraer gracias a la física cuántica
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La gravedad es conocida como una fuerza que atrae objetos, como la Tierra que atrae a la Luna o una manzana que cae de un árbol. Esta idea viene de científicos famosos como Newton y Einstein. Pero aún no se entiende bien cómo funciona la gravedad con objetos muy pequeños, como las partículas.

**Qué pasó** – Dos equipos de investigación de Brasil, Reino Unido e Israel usaron matemáticas para mostrar que, bajo ciertas condiciones cuánticas, la gravedad podría empujar objetos en lugar de atraerlos. Imaginaban una situación donde un objeto muy pequeño toma dos caminos a la vez, una idea extraña de la física cuántica llamada superposición. Otro objeto cercano sentiría la gravedad de forma diferente por esto. Sus cálculos mostraron que si eligen ciertos resultados en el experimento, la gravedad podría volverse repulsiva.

**Impacto** – Esta idea desafía la creencia larga de que la gravedad solo atrae. También sugiere que la gravedad tiene propiedades cuánticas, algo que los científicos han intentado probar durante mucho tiempo. Si se prueba en laboratorio, esto podría cambiar cómo entendemos el universo y abrir nuevas tecnologías basadas en la gravedad cuántica.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren probar esta idea con objetos muy pequeños, del tamaño de bacterias, que puedan mantenerse en superposición el tiempo suficiente para que la gravedad actúe. Estos experimentos son difíciles pero posibles con la tecnología actual. Los científicos ya trabajan con expertos en objetos cuánticos grandes para intentar observar esta gravedad repulsiva.

**Resumen en una frase** – Nuevas investigaciones matemáticas muestran que la física cuántica podría permitir que la gravedad empuje objetos, ofreciendo una forma de probar la naturaleza cuántica de la gravedad en experimentos futuros.
